newsitem.title: UK: The Proteus Column - Lloyd's chain of security..
newsitem.headline: The Proteus Column - Lloyd's chain of security..

text.p: At the presentation to journalists of its global results on Friday, Lloyd's chief executive Ron Sandler was at pains to highlight the enhanced solvency position of the society. He described a "chain of security" consisting of four links - member's premium trust funds, which protect policyholders, the funds at Lloyd's lodged by members to support underwriting, the personal wealth of individual members and the central fund.

Having hived off the bulk of old-business liabilities to Equitas, Sandler was able to show total resources as a percentage of provision for liabilities of 184 percent in 1996, up from 138 percent in 1995.
This week it is expected Lloyd's will publish measures to strengthen security further, including possibly increasing the capital to premium limit ratio required by names to support underwriting.
"We are confident that Lloyd's security ranks amongst the best in the world," Sandler said.

He confirmed too that Lloyd's is seeking an arrangement with ratings agencies such as Standard & Poors and A.M. Best to agree on a single, market-wide solvency rating system that can be used for Lloyd's syndicates.

All these measures are part of the society's campaigns to remove any tarnish from its image, and stem the doubts that began to grow during the loss-making years at Lloyd's despite it never having failed to pay a valid claim.

Already it looks like new business has been coming to Lloyd's and old business returning since the implementation of Reconstruction and Renewal meant the Society's representatives had a good story to tell prospective clients. The fruits of that, despite poor rates, should be looked for in three years' time.

In the meantime, Sandler wants to take the focus away from issues concerning the capital base and put it on customer service. The same phrase is on the lips of every other insurance chief executive, but in the case of Lloyd's there is much that can be done.
In a welcome move, teams from the society's Insurance Services unit and Special Projects are looking for a response to complaints from the U.S. about the time it takes to issues Lloyd's policies.

Delays occur because of complexities stemming from the long chain of brokers who bring business back to Lloyd's and in the difficulties of moving funds up and down the system. Yet it is a fundamental aspect of customer expectations from an insurer which cannot afford to be ignored when the market is so competitive.
The publication of further proposals is awaiting the competition of negotiations with the Lloyd's Insurance Brokers Council and the Insurance Brokers Registration Council.

Finally, the society is now being referred to only as Lloyd's, and not by its fuller title of Lloyd's of London. The reasons for this are vague, and there are several in the society who think it nonsense. As one journalist remarked to the chairman, in the wake of the revamped British Labour Party's recent electoral success, would not have been better to call the society "New Lloyd's"?
